sm: This is the Open to Debate episode recorded at the Masters of Scale Summit, on whether we should stop trusting AI agents with our information. Host John Donvan introduces Meredith Whitaker of Signal arguing not to trust, and Neil Chilson of the Abundance Institute arguing the other side, with Jeff Berman moderating. Whitaker says a consumer agent needs deep, root-level permissions, acts without explicit consent, and treats text as commands, which makes prompt injection a serious hijacking risk. She cites a Copilot data exploit, a hacked Perplexity browser, an eleven percent failure rate in an Anthropic Chrome test, and a calendar attack that switched on a boiler. Chilson says agentic AI flips the old internet bargain, letting people use their own data for tasks once only the wealthy could delegate.

Chilson argues agents do not get bored by inconvenience, so they can read privacy policies and make privacy easier, and he says he used Meta's Muse to opt out of five data brokers with a six-word prompt. Whitaker replies that these agents are not really ours. She describes Muse giving someone's home address to a Marketplace buyer, leaking private company data, and logging contact lists, which implicates people who never installed it. She says giving agents root permissions breaks security sandboxes and that convenience is eating the seed corn of cybersecurity. Chilson answers that the real comparison is the status quo, that trust is conditional on the agent, the use and the access requested, and that he lets agents read online but not write.

Chilson compares agents to messaging, saying society improved platforms rather than abandoning them, and that we learn trust by using these products. Asked about a human assistant, Whitaker says a human is accountable under a labor contract, while agents resemble targeted malware, taking screenshots, running character recognition, sending data off-site, and driving your apps as you. She notes Chase Bank blocked Muse. Chilson says companies have a profit incentive to protect customers, unlike the old ad model. Whitaker says Signal collects no data and so will not launch an agent. She adds that an agent that checks in at every step is hardly an agent, and that the hype should be walked back to technical fundamentals.

Whitaker says screenshotting everything and processing it off-site breaks Signal's security model, and she sees agents as a data grab by big companies, pointing to Amazon's lawsuit against Perplexity. Chilson says no computer or human agent is perfectly safe, that safe depends on safe for what, and that users can tier access, take small steps, and verify. He says all-or-nothing advice will not work, since people without privacy in mind will build the agents otherwise. Whitaker says most people did not know Muse was grabbing contacts. Chilson says an agent could read the fine print for them. In closing, Whitaker says choosing for me is not my choice, and agents hollow out application-level privacy and push power toward large AI companies.

Chilson closes by conceding that sharing your information also shares other people's, but says that is not unique to agents. He says agents will make mistakes, as will companies and users, but we should build them better as was done for messaging, and that opting out of data brokers with one prompt is real privacy protection. He asks the audience to vote no. John Donvan then opens a post-debate conversation, asking each guest about their background. Whitaker says she started at Google in 2006 and watched the data-hungry ad business model grow, including an engineer fired for stalking via an internal dashboard. She read about IBM's role in the Holocaust, and turned to encryption and open-source privacy tools.

Whitaker says large surveillance-driven companies will never apply privacy technology on their own, and that Signal is a nonprofit because there is no business model in collecting no data. Chilson says he was the first in his family to attend college and was drawn to complexity theory, which taught him that complex systems can be influenced but not controlled. He says this makes him wary of grabbing for control and hopeful about empowering individuals, recalling bulletin board systems as a childhood community. He says trade-offs between privacy and convenience differ for each person. Whitaker then explains prompt injection: agents cannot tell authentic text from malicious text, such as hidden white text on a website telling the agent to run malware.

Whitaker says an injected agent can be made to leak data, share a home address, or publish private letters. She notes the Anthropic Chrome test's eleven percent failure rate and says the UK's National Cyber Security Centre warned prompt injection may never be solved. She repeats the calendar attack that made an agent turn on a boiler and open shutters. Chilson says defense in depth, with input filters, back-end permission controls, and training, can make agents safer, as happened with computer viruses in the nineties. He says there is no hundred percent safety, and these are engineering problems. Whitaker asks who the we is, and says the burden of care should fall on trillion-dollar companies, not on users as guinea pigs.

Chilson says companies are legally liable for most of these harms and face scrutiny from law and investors, so incentives exist to fix problems, though liability rules might be tweaked. He says the answer is to tackle challenges, not stop the technology. Whitaker agrees agents are useful for coding, where results are verifiable, but says her concern is consumer agents that hollow out security architecture and concentrate data in the hands of existing AI winners. She says the question is trust, not convenience, and the evidence says they are not trustworthy. Chilson says trustworthy depends on the task. He trusts agents with many things but not moving money, and he compares agents to washing machines and the early internet as technologies with trade-offs.

Whitaker says trusting an agent with one mundane task still gives it the key to everything, and that a few prompt injections later it is in the dresser drawers. She says an agent that checks in every time is not an agent as the term is used today. Chilson says Muse runs in Meta's cloud, which isolates it from a user's own computer, and that the address went to a real buyer, so users are still learning how to charge an agent with a task. Asked about solutions, Whitaker says she does not want to stop agents. She says a reckless rush driven by huge AI spending is casting aside cybersecurity basics, citing a Hugging Face incident, Copilot data leaks, and a PHP bug.

Chilson says the worst examples are in coding, the first frontier where defenders must be given the advantage. He agrees we need more coordination, more research, and clear accountability, so companies cannot blame their agents, and says some gaps in current law should be filled. Asked about the debate experience, Whitaker says she was not trying to win points but is alarmed at people forgetting technical fundamentals. Chilson says the applause favored her, he had just attended a conference of AI doomers, and that he sees the answer as incentives and empowering people, not doom or central control. Donvan closes with the voting information and says this is the first of several AI debates, with education and deepfakes next.
